input:
In this work, the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde was investigated, with the aim of comparing two different catalyst forms under identical conditions. The performance of each catalyst was characterised in terms of its space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). All of the tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3 and a single feed composition, so that the two catalysts could be compared on a consistent basis.

The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.98 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.24 bar and an activity loss of 7% after 100 h on stream. The pellet catalyst, by contrast, gave a considerably lower space-time yield of 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, together with a much higher pressure drop of 1.14 bar and an activity loss of 20% after 100 h. The structured form therefore outperformed the pellet form on all three of the measures reported here, delivering more product per unit volume while imposing a smaller pressure penalty and retaining more of its initial activity over the test period.

It should nevertheless be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so the tolerance of either catalyst to sulfur remains unknown. In addition, yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature, which makes it difficult to place these results in a broader context. Within the conditions actually tested, however, the comparison clearly favours the structured catalyst, and any extrapolation beyond the single feed composition used here should be made with caution.
target:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde, and two catalyst forms were compared at one feed composition, at 280 °C and 40 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3. Performance is stated as space-time yield, the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), with pressure drop and activity loss reported for the same charges.

The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.98 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 7% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.14 bar, and an activity loss of 20% after 100 h. The structured form is higher on yield and lower on both penalties at the tested conditions; the comparison is between the two forms as charged, and yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge elsewhere, which limits the outside comparisons that can be drawn.

Space-time yield is the measure that sizes the reactor: at a fixed duty, the form with the higher yield needs the smaller catalyst volume, and the structured form's advantage on pressure drop compounds in the same direction, since the charge that produces more per unit volume also resists the flow less. The two advantages point the same way here, which is not guaranteed in general: a form can win on yield and lose on pressure drop, and a comparison that reports only one of the two leaves the trade-off invisible.

No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so neither form's tolerance to sulfur is known, and a feed carrying sulfur would test a property this comparison does not reach. The preference for the structured catalyst is a preference at the tested conditions and at the single feed composition used; a second feed composition, richer or leaner, could move the pressure drop and the activity loss in different proportions for the two forms, and the ranking is not claimed beyond the conditions that produced it.
